questions.prompt: An HTML response uses an enforced CSP `script-src` containing a nonce. How should its server generate that nonce?

sources.title: Content Security Policy Level 3
sources.claim: CSP requires a fresh, unpredictable nonce for each policy transmission. A user identifier, filename or reused fixed value lets an attacker predict or reuse authorization.

questions.explanation: CSP requires a fresh, unpredictable nonce for each policy transmission. A user identifier, filename or reused fixed value lets an attacker predict or reuse authorization.

choices.text: Derive a predictable value from the current user account.
Reuse one fixed secret value across all HTML responses.
Use the script filename as a stable authorization value.
Generate a fresh, unpredictable value for each response.

questions.prompt: A script integrity attribute contains valid SHA-256 and SHA-384 metadata. Its bytes match only the SHA-256 value. What does SRI verification do?

sources.title: Subresource Integrity
sources.claim: Verification uses the strongest supported metadata algorithm. A weaker matching SHA-256 digest does not rescue the SHA-384 mismatch. There is no automatic insecure retry.

questions.explanation: Verification uses the strongest supported metadata algorithm. A weaker matching SHA-256 digest does not rescue the SHA-384 mismatch. There is no automatic insecure retry.

choices.text: Reject the resource because the stronger digest does not match.
Accept the resource because any listed digest is sufficient to match.
Accept the resource because SHA-256 is checked before stronger hashes.
Download the script again without integrity metadata to resolve the mismatch.

questions.prompt: In a browser supporting Trusted Types, an enforced CSP includes `require-trusted-types-for 'script'`, and no default policy exists. Which statements hold? Select all that apply.

sources.title: Trusted Types
sources.claim: A and B: enforcement rejects strings at covered HTML injection sinks and accepts the matching trusted type. E: policy callbacks must enforce safety. C is false because callbacks are application code; D is false because enforcement targets specified sinks, not every property.

questions.explanation: A and B: enforcement rejects strings at covered HTML injection sinks and accepts the matching trusted type. E: policy callbacks must enforce safety. C is false because callbacks are application code; D is false because enforcement targets specified sinks, not every property.

choices.text: Assigning a plain string to `innerHTML` can throw a TypeError.
A policy-created `TrustedHTML` can satisfy an HTML injection sink.
Creating a policy guarantees that its callback sanitizes every input.
The policy requirement automatically applies to every string property.
The application still must design safe policy transformations.

questions.prompt: A page enforces `script-src 'nonce-random123'` without other script sources. Which inline script is authorized by this policy?

sources.title: Content Security Policy Level 3
sources.claim: The nonce-source matches the script nonce value exactly. An id, filename or arbitrary nonce cannot substitute for that value.

questions.explanation: The nonce-source matches the script nonce value exactly. An id, filename or arbitrary nonce cannot substitute for that value.

choices.text: A script whose nonce attribute is `random123`.
A script with a matching `id` but no nonce attribute.
A script with an empty nonce and an identical filename.
A script with any nonce because a nonce source exists.

questions.prompt: A script has two supported SHA-384 integrity values and its bytes match one of them. What is the digest-verification result?

sources.title: Subresource Integrity
sources.claim: Within the strongest algorithm, matching any one metadata digest passes. SRI neither requires all alternatives to match nor concatenates their values.

questions.explanation: Within the strongest algorithm, matching any one metadata digest passes. SRI neither requires all alternatives to match nor concatenates their values.

choices.text: The bytes fail because every listed strongest-algorithm value must match.
The bytes pass because one strongest-algorithm value matches.
The bytes fail because multiple values disable integrity verification.
The bytes pass only after both digest values are concatenated and hashed.

questions.prompt: A team wraps untrusted input in a Trusted Types policy before using `innerHTML`. Which security conclusions are valid? Select all that apply.

sources.title: Trusted Types
sources.claim: A: safe transformation belongs in the policy. C: the object reflects policy creation, not proof of harmless content. B and D are false because Trusted Types does not automatically sanitize or repair application code. E is false because the trusted wrapper does not prove the callback was safe.

questions.explanation: A: safe transformation belongs in the policy. C: the object reflects policy creation, not proof of harmless content. B and D are false because Trusted Types does not automatically sanitize or repair application code. E is false because the trusted wrapper does not prove the callback was safe.

choices.text: The policy callback must apply an appropriate safety transformation.
Returning the input unchanged automatically strips unsafe HTML markup.
The returned trusted object records passage through the policy.
Trusted Types automatically repairs every unsafe sanitizer configuration.
Producing TrustedHTML proves that the callback removed every dangerous construct.
